subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, April 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Max D. Cormier for an address to His Excellency the Administrator in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, In resuming my remarks on the address, interrupted by the adjournment of Tuesday evening, I draw your attention once more to what the speech from the throne says concerning cooperation and unity in Canada. I repeat the quotation:
In prosperity they were united. In adversity that union is made still stronger by the spirit of cooperation and mutual understanding which is the surest bulwark of the nation's welfare and happiness.
The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who is the author of the speech from the throne and who put these fine phrases into the mouth of His Excellency has not, in the past, practised what he preaches. Did the right hon. Prime Minister and his Conservative followers preach union, cooperation and mutual understanding for the safeguarding of Canada's welfare and happiness during the last campaign? They did not. Wherever they addressed public meetings, before election day, our opponents went to unbelievable lengths of crowd-baiting in their determination to uproot the people's trust in those who had governed the country for the past ten years. They showed the situation in a false light, they appealed to prejudice, they stirred up the most baneful leanings of the populace; they went so far as to twist public opinion in a very harmful way. Were they striving thus to ensure the happiness of Canada's citizens?
The Address-Mr. Parent

I state it as my sincere belief that this spirit of harmony and confidence was the result of ten years of good government under the prosperous Liberal regime.
The speech from the throne goes on:
These attributes of Canadianism are national assets of real value, and, upon their possession, I do profoundly congratulate you.
This paragraph of the speech from the throne makes His Excellency pay a well-deserved tribute to the Liberal party who endowed our people with these national assets of Canadianism.
Mr. Speaker, these "attributes of Canadianism" are in large part due to the policy of peace and harmony of the Liberal administration, unfailing in their consideration and respect towards minority groups in matters' of language, of education and of creed.
Canadianism is a word pregnant with meaning, like patriotism, like "Canada First"; but it is upheld by acts, by deeds; it is not an empty cry and, mayhap, a deceitful one.
Mr. Speaker, Canadianism is to be found only among those who understand and truly observe the prerogatives handed down to us under the British flag which every Canadian subject is proud to wave beside our own national emblem.
Where is the Canadianism of our Conservative friends? Let us take as a sample these biting words, born of hate and anger, uttered by the right hon. Prime Minister on June 10th, at Calgary, and reported in the Leader Post. Speaking of the Liberals, he had this to say:
They make a plaything of people's lives, why? Do they realize that they are playing with lives, with food for women and children, with hunger? Nine years of wasted effort before the great betrayal. Judas took less time.
Mr. Speaker, is that preaching union, cooperation and mutual understanding to the country?
Or, take what he said of the Liberal party at the outset of the election campaign:
This group of mercenaries who hang on to power through sham and subterfuge, look upon them as traitors to your cause.
When a political leader uses such language, which is beneath his dignity, is he upholding the spirit of cooperation and mutual among the citizens of his country? Is this sort of low spell-binding the proper method for safeguarding the welfare and the happiness of a nation, does it enhance respect for authority? To excuse the author we would fain believe that he had lost control of himself when he used those regrettable words.

Why all this anger, all this hatred, merely to win votes in an election? At any rate, these unfortunate words may very well unleach the passions of the masses and destroy all respect for authority; and the day when the people will have lost all respect for constituted authority, the gates will be thrown wide open to communism and to bolshevism. Such language has never before, to my know-' ledge, fallen from the lips of a political leader who wished to be respected; apologies are in order. I ask the presumed author of these words, the right hon. Prime Minister, to specify what members of the Liberal party deserve the opprobrious epithet of Judas. Mr. Speaker, there is no Judas in the Liberal party.
I deplore this excess of language, I consider it an insult to a great many Canadian citizens; and I repeat that the insult should be withdrawn, I trust the author will withdraw the epithet " Judas ", I suggest to the right hon. Prime Minister that he seek out the Judases in our political life and that he obtain the cooperation of his colleague from Mont-magny (Mr. LaVergne) who has some knowledge in the matter.
One after another the Conservative candidates and the right hon. Prime Minister proclaimed throughout the length and breadth of Canada, during the last campaign, that the Liberals had ruined the country through their carelessness; that the Liberals were to blame for the economic depression, for the unemployment crisis; that our industries were going to the wall, that trade was stagnant; that foreign markets must be found for our farm produce, that an outlet for our western wheat was imperative, and they added: "Elect us to office and we will soon set matters straight, or perish in the attempt." That is what they said before the election, Mr. Speaker, to win the people's votes. But all these statements were contradicted by the hon. ministers of the crown themselves, once the elections were over. As proof of this I intend quoting to the house a paper published not in Canada but in Japan. They went quite a distance from Canada to tell the truth after the election.
I have now to revert to the English language.
I have in my hand the front page of a journal published in Japan under the title of the Japan Times and Mail. This is what it has to say under date of Monday, October 27, 1930:
Canada's Export Trade Stands on a Firm Foundation.
Each year it grows in the volume and in importance to every community in the Dominion.

The Address-Mr. Parent
Export business provides millions of Canadians with their livelihood. Nearly a third of Canada's annual production is shipped to other
Each year the volume grows. From $740,000,000 in 1922, it has grown to $1,363,700,000 in 1929. For the first ten months of 1929 the export of manufactured and partly manufactured goods has increased by $46,500,000, while the export of raw material has decreased by $70,700,000.
In foreign lands the demand for our goods and products is at a premium.
I shall not quote further from this journal, because to do so would use up all my time, but it would be very interesting if the article could be published in the newspapers of the Dominion so that every Canadian could take cognizance of it.
(Translation) Mr. Speaker, this happened a few days after the election. And I beg you to note that this advertisement was published by the department of Trade and Commerce under the signature of the present hon. minister in the Bennett cabinet (Mr.Stevens), and that of his deputy; so that the statement is authentic, and it flatly contradicts what all the Conservatives and all the members of the government were saying all through the country during the campaign, in their efforts to mislead the people. After the election our Conservative friends discover that Canada's foreign trade is prosperous.
If this Japanese paper had been shown to the voters in different ridings, in Quebec province and elsewhere, in East Kootenay, for instance, or Chambly-Vercheres, Two Mountains, Montmagny or other constituencies, would the hon. members of the government occupy a seat in this house, I wonder. But there is more to come. I am going to quote another hon. minister; not what he said on the floor of the house; so far most of the ministers have abstained from addressing parliament; one is lead to imagine that silence is enjoined upon the hon. ministers in the House of Commons. Listen to what the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) had to say in clubs and at banquets. In November 1930, speaking at a banquet given by the Sauve club in the Mount Royal Hotel, the hon. minister, after telling of Canada's wealth, went on to say:
Canada leads the world in agricultural products. It is second in importance among the manufacturing countries of the empire; first in the export of wheat, newsprint, nickel, asbestos; first in national wealth per capita.
There you have the truth, Mr. Speaker but it flatly contradicts the assertions of his leader and of all the Conservative candidates in the course of last summer's campaign. If the
hon. Minister of Marine had been as accurate with the voters of Chambly-Vercheres, would he be an "honourable" to-day?
Coming back to the speech from the throne,
I quote further:
The fact that in this period of universal distress Canada has been spared the same acute degree of hardship which many other nations have been called upon to bear, will not, I know, blind you to the fact that between this country as it is and as it should be, there is a gulf to be bridged by the industry and zeal of all those who have the welfare of the nation in their keeping.
The situation has changed, says His Excellency in the speech from the throne. Indeed there have been changes, Mr. Speaker, since our Conservative friends came into power! Let us glance at a few eloquent figures which go to prove this. I am speaking now of the adverse change in the export of our domestic products. In January 1930, under a Liberal government, our exports were valued at $73,000,000; in January 1931, under the Conservatives, this had fallen to $44,000,000: a reduction of 30 percent. In February 1930, under the Liberals, $66,000,000; in February 1931 under the Conservatives, $43,000,000 :	30 per
cent less. We are told that the national treasury faces a deficit of $100,000,000; quite a change from the surpluses built up by the Liberal administration. The government have to borrow to make up the deficit: the Liberals were constantly reducing our national indebtedness. We may expect an increase in taxes; tax reduction was the order when the Liberals were in office. There has been a pronounced weakening in the prices the farmer receives for his produce, just the opposite of what the Conservatives promised and foretold when they were out looking for votes. Canadian products, our agricultural products in particular, have lost nearly all their foreign markets, thanks to our exorbitant tariff increases. Canada is no longer a ranking nation in the matter of export trade.
In a word the change has been much for the worse; the situation fosters foreboding and causes much more uneasiness than did the crisis at election time.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne asks us to set ourselves zealously to the task of filling this void; it says that certain factors of a domestic character were responsible for our present economic ills. I ask the honourable members on the other side to point out to us, if they can, what domestic factors contributed to this trade depression. They will try to make us believe that the Liberal administration is to blame for the sorry state of affairs brought about by the loss of our foreign markets. My reply is that it was the Liberals
The Address-Mr. Parent

who opened up these markets for our Canadian products and that the markets have been lost since the Conservative party came into power. And I quote, as proof, the statement of a man whose authority and knowledge in the matter is unquestioned. The general manager of the Bank of Nova Scotia, speaking before the general meeting of the shareholders, in Montreal, on January 28th, 1931, said what follows:
In ten years the proportion of Canadian products sold in foreign markets had increased from 25 to 30 per cent.
This was under the Liberal regime, since 1921. The gentlemen opposite must agree that times are changed indeed! In its monthly letter, published recently, the Bank of Montreal points out Canada's foreign trade has decreased by 36 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, we should look for the cause of all our ills in the action of the present government: they boosted the customs tariff to such a height that other countries refused to go on buying Canadian products, since we no longer bought theirs. We are isolating ourselves, that is what it amounts to; and Canada is producing a surplus of manufactured and agricultural products which we cannot sell abroad, to such an extent has our foreign trade fallen off. Prices are tumbling, factories are laying off their hands, unemployment is on the increase. There you have the fruits of a high protective policy.
The members to your right, Mr. Speaker, realizing the disastrous results of their shortsighted policy, and the terrible pass to W'hich they have brought the country, are seemingly bent on appealing to clairvoyants.
I quote for you what was said by the honourable Minister of Marine,.at that same banquet tendered by the "Club Sauve", in Montreal, on the 27th of last November, as reported in La Presse. He had just spoken of the hardships people were undergoing in a rich country like Canada; he continued thus: We needed a clairvoyant mind, a man of action who would know how to give form and expression to the people's thought.
And he mentioned Mr. Bennett's name.

A message was delivered by Major A. R. Thompson, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:

I ask the hon. Minister of Marine to tell us when he speaks on the floor of the house-and we are anxious to hear him-just what the present government has done for Canada since it came into power. I suppose his reply will be: protection. I maintain that the protective policy shackles foreign trade, that it has prevented the sale of our manufactured products to the detriment of the consuming public, the farmers, especially, who have to pay high prices for everything they buy, while their own products must be sold on a steadily weakening market; the farmers' candle is being burned at both ends.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that agriculture, a3 the basic industry of this country, should receive first consideration at the hands of our government, before any other group.
I believe that if the hon. Minister of Marine's "clairvoyant" had foretold the present condition of the farming class in Chambly-Vercheres, Two Mountains, and other Quebec constituencies, we would have fewer Conservative representatives in this house to-day.
If the hon. Minister of Marine answers: "Unemployment relief," I will quote him the words spoken by the right hon. Prime Minister at Victoria on the 16th of June last ("Colonist"):
Is there any excuse for hard times in this country, if the government does its duty?
and at Sarnia on July 16th ("Mail and Empire") :
Someone is responsible for unemployment; not individuals but the government. Because of their majorities in parliament governments must answer for every bit of legislation passed.
I grant you that the government passed a law for the relief of unemployment. But what

The Address-Mr. Fortin
does it amount to? I state here and now that the government did not beep their promise to end unemployment; they did not assume the share of liability they pledged themselves to assume under the unemployment relief act. They threw all the burden on the municipalities; most of the latter were unable to negotiate loans and to contribute an equivalent amount to that put up by the federal and provincial treasuries. That is not what was promised on the campaign platform.

(Translation) Mr. Speaker, from my seat in this house, I wish to pay a tribute to my constituents in Levis I wish to tell them how I appreciate the honour they conferred upon me when electing me as their representative, and that they can rely on my unremitted devotion at all times.
In rising to speak for the first time in this house, I do so with a deep feeling, as I happen to be the first Conservative member returned by the constituency of Levis since 1882. This feeling is easily accountable for when I recollect that I have been called upon to succeed the Hon. Dr. Blanchet, grandfather of the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), who is the minister from my district. As I am thus evoking the memory of my illustrious predecessor w'ho so fittingly occupied the chair you now adorn, Mr. Speaker, it is indeed my pleasure to offer to you my congratulations for your election to that office.
I desire to extend my felicitations to my fellow countrymen who, in delivering their speeches in their mother tongue have set the example, and had I a reproach to express, it would be addressed to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), and even to the hon. deputy speaker of this house (Mr. LaVergne), who could at least have delivered part of their speeches in French. However, upon further thought, I felt that the hon. deputy speaker had used the English language in order that his remarks might be understood and to defend us more efficiently. I take this opportunity to express the hope that our esteemed deputy speaker shall speedily recover from his illness. I wish to inform him that his valuable help shall still be required in our national contests. Norris was the idol of the Liberals, even of the French Canadian
The Address-Mr. Fortin

Liberals, but ourselves, we shall stand up against Anderson. And it is my sincere wish that the hon. prime minister of Saskatchewan may remember that we have at Rideau Hall a lady of the manor of French origin.
I was rather shocked, if I may use the term, when I was asked by several members, Liberal and Conservative, from Ontario and other provinces, where the constituency of Levis was located and other information concerning same. For a few moments, let me take you on a journey through my constituency. The county of Levis is separated from Quebec by the St. Lawrence river. It has two means of communication; first, the Quebec bridge, and in second place, the ferry service. When reaching Levis from the ferry boats the first building to be seen, and that is rather significant, is the Canada National Railway station; we also see the up-to-date customs house, and on our left, the yards from which coal is being shipped to all parts of the province of Quebec. A few steps farther, one may board a street car of the Levis Tramways Company and proceed to Lauzon where are located the famous Lome and Champlain dry docks. You may know or may not know that the Lome and Champlain dry docks are the most up-to-date in the world; at this same place may be seen also the shipyards where skilled workmen are now	engaged	in	building, for the	Canadian	National	Railways,	a car ferry ofsome	500 feet	in	length.	It was on	behalfof these workers, that, at the first caucus held	during the	special	session, I	called
the attention of the Prime Minister and of the Minister from my district (Mr. Dupre) to the opportunity of exacting a duty of 25 per cent on all foreign naval construction. Quite recently, I noticed in a newspaper that a manufacturer, more experienced than myself, had suggested that we should follow the example of the United States and apply a duty of 50 per cent. At the caucus above mentioned I was promised-and the Conservatives, as a rule, keep their promises

that action would be taken accordingly, and the matter was discussed at the interprovincial conference held recently.
Let us leave the Lome and Champlain dry docks and proceed to the military camp at Lauzon, where the various regiments of the Quebec district hold their annual drills. This camp has been in existence for a great many years and it is surrounded with old forts that are now classified as historical sites, but which ought to be kept in a better condition by the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland) for I would be

ashamed to ask tourists to pay a visit to these forts.
Thence, we proceed to the armouries which are the general headquarters of the Quebec and Levis regiments. We then go to the Quarantine where is disembarked the grade live stock imported from foreign countries. A little further on, one may see the Breakey-ville mills and those of the Gravel Lumber Company, and some distance away the large Canadian National Railways workshops, of great size, forsooth, but unfortunately idle. If the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) was at his seat-

This is the point from which, after our journey through the county, we retrace our steps via the well known Quebec bridge. It is to be hoped that the mention of the famous Quebec bridge shall bring to mind the constituency of Levis and that I shall no longer meet people saying to me: Where is the county of Levis? The county of Levis has also given the country quite a number of men of great distinction. Many of them went through the College of Levis, from which both the hon. parish of my constituency. And lastly, I could not overlook our national bard, Louis Frechette.
Speaking of my Alma Mater, I wish to bring out the fact the college of Levis has made for itself quite a reputation in the intercollegiate contests held for some years back. Twelve students from our Alma Mater were awarded the Prince of Wales prize.
The unfortunate thing about the constituency of Levis is its close proximity to Quebec, as well as its being included within the boundaries of Quebec harbour. When it comes to secure a construction or improvement of some kind, complications arise. Only recently, having come to the conclusion that a deep water wharf would be of great advantage, the electors for Levis petitioned me to that end. Before applying to the place where I expected a favourable reply, I had to visit several offices.
I was first asked to see the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) who, after a delay of three or four weeks, told me that he could not deal with the matter owing to the fact that Levis is within the boundaries of Quebec harbour and that the Minister of Public Works has no authority to undertake any work there. A few days later, I went to the Department of Marine and there I was told by the hon. Minister (Mr. Duranleau): "Go and see the harbour commissioners and have the matter settled by the chairman and manager of that board." In other words his advice to me was that I should go and solicit from the president and manager of that board a favour which they mean to keep to themselves. I may state, Mr. Speaker, that for the last twenty-five years we have asked for deep water piers at Levis and the matter is of the utmost importance, it being the key to the successful development of our industrial and commercial establishments.
Recently I had a conversation with the Hon. Senator Lemieux who said:	"Levis
is a splendid county, Levis is a beautiful city, but when one comes to the lower part of the town, the sight of its dilapidated wharves is disgraceful." In reply, I said to him: "I took steps in order to have this state of affairs remedied." I may be too pessimistic in my forebodings, though I have not seen anything in the estimates; otherwise I might lose the sympathy of the minister representing my district; however, I have not lost hope of succeeding for, as the hon. member for Dorchester was telling me the other day: "The supplementary estimates are yet to come."
The deep water wharves in question would only cost a trifle as compared to the $20,000,000 that have been spent in the harbour of
Quebec. This work being requested not only by Levis but by the south shore, by the constituencies of Bellechasse, Dorchester, Lot-biniere and Beauce, it seems to me that the government ought to grant my request.
My predecessors, Mr. Speaker, have not neglected their duty. I am aware that they applied to the government for the very thing I am asking for this day, but always without success. If, as a member for Levis, I must make requests and never secure anything, I say frankly that it is not my intention to act as a footstool to those who have political ambitions.

You have given to the entire country a magnificent lesson in bonne entente. You have, moreover, made it clear that the language that is dear to you will work side by side with our own mother tongue, in
Canada as in the League of Nations, for peace, harmony and fraternity among the different racial groups who go to make up this Canadian nation.
I followed with very great interest also the speech of the hon. member for Res-tigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Cormier). His exposition of Conservative policy was more than a profession of faith in a political doctrine: he showed the whole country that Memramcook College, an institution which numbers him among her most brilliant graduates, endows her students, as do all our French colleges in Canada, with a bilingual education. His presence here in this house is proof, moreover, of the survival of the French group who, since the great disturbance, have never ceased, from the plains of Acadia to the most remote bayous of Louisiana, to grow in numbers and in influence.
The seconder of the address also belongs to the new generation of public men who refuse to believe that parliamentary custom is something which cannot be changed. The designated mover of the address made way for the honourable member for Restigouche. This gesture, truly Canadian, is a sign of the times. There is no question of racial superiority in Canada; and I would be happy to know that in the future this rotation will be an established thing in the House of Commons.
The debate has been mild, Mr. Speaker, particularly amongst us French-Canadians from Quebec, representing the two political groups of the province. If an epithet has been dropped here and there, from one side or the other, if there has been a little teasing, it has all been couched in that genuine politeness which drew from one English governor the opinion that we were "a race of gentlemen".
There must be a debate, Mr. Speaker. Was it not the fabulist Lafontaine who wrote: "Discussion is a valuable help; without it we would sleep through life"?
Before entering into a discussion of the respective merits, or demerits, of the speech from the throne, let us glance at the conservative platform whence came all the speeches of the last election campaign.
At the last session of 1930 the two main features of the Conservative program were discussed on the floor of this house, our opponents refused to recognize that unemployment was an international problem and they claimed that the butter problem-God knows the province of Quebec was covered with butter during the last campaign-was due to the carelessness of the William Lyon Mac-

kenzie King administration. I must frankly admit that our Conservative friends were well prepared. The right hon. Prime Minister did me the honour of opening his campaign in a Montreal district, next to my riding. I listened attentively to his speech, over the radio, in my humble home. He appealed to the unemployed; he surely intended to kill two birds with one stone, speaking in Maisonneuve county, adjacent to Hochelaga; but the workers in these two electoral districts gave a negative answer to the Conservative party, and your humble servant and the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Robitaille) won the support of the voters once more, to the cause of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, to the cause of the Liberal party which, of all the political parties, has most often bent down to humble folk and lent them a helping hand.

He asked him, particularly, if he pledged himself to build in Canada the ships Canada needed. The Hon. Mr. Bennett replied that he saw no Objection to that. But I am still wondering where those ships are, since most of the former employees of the Vickers shipyard are still without work.

Coming
as I do from one of the older rural constituencies in western Canada, I desire to make a few observations.
I have listened with a good deal of interest to the debate so far, and particularly to the h'On. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins); and without in any way reflecting on that honourable gentlemen or the constituency he represents, permit me to say that the constituency of Macdonald is quite as good a constituency as Marquette, and in many respects better. The electors are just as intelligent, and there are very few, if any, cowless, sowless, chickenless farms.
I would like to indicate briefly to this house the very definite efforts the farmers of Macdonald constituency are making towards stabilizing their agricultural business, and I think it applies equally well to the rest of Manitoba.
It may not be generally known that the first bovine tuberculosis free area to be established in the British Empire was established in the constituency of Macdonald a few years ago. This area has served as the centre from which several agricultural activities of far-reaching importance have been developed. It has gradually been extended both locally as well as in other parts of Canada. This same area has for some time been recognized as an improved sire area, and when the provincial government introduced its system of agricultural representative, it was one of the first to take advantage of it. There have for many years been established sire clubs of one kind or another, making possible the securing of the best sires in the country in a cooperative way.
Very tangible evidence of the efforts of the farmers of my constituency can be gleaned

from the recent exhibition held in the city of Brandon. In looking over the list of prize-winnings in grains and grasses, fully 25 per cent have been won by farmers in Macdonald constituency; including the championship in barley, won by Mr. John Wiener of Miami,-a member of the Miami Cooperative Barley Growers Association. A similar honor was won by Mr. George Knox of the same place at the Toronto Royal last fall. The farmers of Miami district have for years paid particular attention to producing high quality barley for malting purposes as well as for seed, and have annually some 40,000, to 60,000 bushels for sale.
Looking further afield, one can note that the farmers of Manitoba have established a very enviable reputation in the larger Canadian and American exhibitions in winning more than their share of the prizes. Manitoba butter-makers have a most enviable reputation in the larger butter shows of Canada, the creameries of Macdonald constituency being well among the winners as well as the Manitoba cooperative dairies. The honey producers of Manitoba have established for Manitoba honey a reputation that is second to none in the world.
In the matter of quality hog production Manitoba stands high. Car lots of bacon hogs selected from the products of the boys' and girls' clubs, as well as of individual exhibitors, have been consistent winners at the Toronto Royal. And I venture the assertion that there is not another area in western Canada that consistently ships to the market as high a percentage of bacon type hogs as does the constituency of Macdonald.
I do not mean to imply that the farmers of Manitoba or the constituency of Macdonald have reached perfection as regards quality production, but I do say they are doing their part, and that the farmers of this older, longer established district should be in as good a position as any farmers in western Canada to withstand this period of depression.
I am setting out these facts to indicate that so far as the farmers of my constituency are concerned they are at least doing their part. They are producing high quality products which the markets of the world demand and it is only fair for them to say to the governments of this country, both provincial and dominion: "We are doing our part. What are you going to do for us?"
We have, however, areas even in Macdonald constituency quite unsuited for live stock, and one area in particular that presents a serious problem on account of drainage. Three years ago the people there could not put in a crop because of flood conditions.

The Address-t-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
The next year they got in their crop but could not take it oS because of water lying in their fields. Many farmers had to bring their stock into the bams during the month of August and to keep it there until such time as the water receded. As an indication of what these flood conditions mean, I might state that the Sperling cooperative elevator handled in 1927 approximately 400,000 bushels of grain while for the following two years that mark was reduced to something in the neighbourhod of 100,000 bushels, and much of that had to be resold locally for seed and feed. This district now has drainage facilities but their installation has increased taxes to such an extent that the farmers cannot carry the load under present conditions. That problem will have to be handled by someone very soon or one of the best wheat growing areas in western Canada will be abandoned.
Strange as it may seem, so far as live stock production is concerned, even considering the flood conditions during certain seasons, this area has no permanent supply of water for stock. There are no wells, creeks or rivers; they have to depend wholly upon dug-outs for their water supply, which I think everyone will agree does not offer an adequate or reliable supply for mixed farming.
I venture the assertion that the farmers as a whole have put in a reasonably good winter. I do not suppose that very many on the farms have suffered from hunger during the past few months, nor do I suppose that many have suffered from the cold; but it has been a mild winter. One coal dealer told me that hi3 business had been reduced some 50 per cent during this last winter. So far as the farmers in my district are concerned, they have spent very little for clothes or anything which was not absolutely necessary. In the majority of cases, any money spent for ordinary living expenses was money which should have gone to pay taxes and interest on mortgage indebtedness.
During the past six or eight months I have met many farmers, who have pioneered this country, established good homes, educated their families, and contributed much to their local communities as well as to the country as a whole. I am sorry to say that these same men, ordinarily considered as well established, successful farmers, are greatly concerned and worried at the present time. They tell me that they are unable to pay their taxes or their interest charges and that the banks are reluctant to loan them money. They inquire as to the advisability of putting in a crop; they say that in the main they can put in a crop but they cannot afford to take a loss again this year as they have for

the past two years. Their greatest concern, Mr. Speaker, is their lack of security in their homes and holdings. Homes they have spent a lifetime in building up are subject to such mortgage indebtedness that they are fearful of being dispossessed. That is what is bothering the western farmer at the present time.
Is it any wonder then that the farmers are Baking what this government is going to do for them? They see tariffs raised to help the manufacturer, and money paid out for unemployment relief, and they naturally want to know what the government is going to do with respect to agriculture. Before Christmas I was telling these men to wait until December 30, but since that time I have been forced to say that I do not know what the government's policy is going to be. These men do not want to put in another crop under uncertain conditions and they are still waiting for an announcement from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) or from some other member of the government as to what the policy of the government is going to be in respect to agriculture.
The situation confronting the western farmer is one that requires the most serious consideration on the part of this government and something must be done immediately^ in order to renew his confidence-something that will have immediate effect. To that end I feel it is essential that our Dominion and provincial governments give assurance without delay that they will protect the farmer in the security of his home and holding. To that end, it may be necessary to declare some form of moratorium. Of course, that is only delaying the evil day but it may serve the purpose until something else can be done or until world conditions improve. It would give the farmer a renewal of confidence and courage and enable him to carry on.
As a second measure of relief, I wish to associate myself with those who have already contributed to this debate in urging a reduction of interest rates. It is the accumulation of debt that is bearing down the western farmer; it is interest added to principal and interest on principal and interest added to that again. The farmer has been obliged to carry the whole load of this depression without being able to pass it on. A reduction in interest charges would mean much to him and in the long run I think it would mean a good deal to those people from whom he has borrowed.
As a further suggestion, I would associate myself with those hon. members who have been urging a reduction in our domestic freight rates, particularly on the shipment of

I would urge upon the Minister of Agriculture the necessity of doing something towards assisting the marketing of hogs next fall. The farmers of western Canada this summer have gone extensively into hog raising and there will be a tremendous increase in hog production by next fall. They have attempted to use up their low priced feed grains, and in this they have been encouraged .by local institutions, including the banks, the mortgage companies, the railways and the governments.
I think it is essential that our Department of Agriculture come forward with some scheme
IMr. W. G. Weir.]
which would assist in the marketing next fall of the largely increased supply of live hogs. If the minister can offer a scheme which will assist this situation, I, for one, will lend him my wholehearted support.
Just here I should like to emphasize the remarks made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) in respect to an agricultural policy, particularly that part where she states:
All farm or agricultural colleges should to-day teach cooperative marketing of farm products as aggressively as in the past they taught, and are still teaching, greater production. As the central idea of their programs they should have cooperative marketing of farm products, and the government should lend its full moral support to any efforts made along the lines of cooperation.
Those are exactly my sentiments. I do not think a successful agricultural policy can be established that does not take into consideration (the actual producers on the land, nor do I think any agricultural policy can be successfully carried out that does not return to the producers the highest possible proportion of the price which the consumer has to pay.
The farmers of Manitoba are looking to the government to see that Fort Churchill has a fair opportunity to operate particularly in respect of rail rates to and from Churchill as well as ocean rates and marine insurance. As a further effort to develop trade at Churchill, the advisability of making it a free port might be taken into consideration. I understand that it costs from S100 to 81,200 for harbour dues at some of our larger ocean poi'ts, and if charges like those are made to apply at Churchill, this would impose quite a heavy burden upon the boats using that port. If, on the other hand, this being a wholly government-owned port, the government could forego those charges, at least in the initial stages of the development of the port, that would go a long way toward developing trade there and perhaps have favourable effect on ocean rates to and from Churchill.
In closing, let me repeat what I said at the beginning: the farmers in my constituency, which is one of the oldest constituencies of the province, are doing their part honestly and conscientiously-and I know the same is true of the farmers of the whole of Manitoba as well as of western Canada- but they are not going to be able to carry on for very long under present conditions. In fact, some of them have not been able to carry on thus far. The government has given assistance to the manufacturers and to

At that election Mr. Ferguson was returned, not merely with 50 per cent of the elected members as Conservatives, but with over 70 per cent of the elected members supporting him and his policies. He carried on for another term of three years and again appealed to the electors of the province of Ontario. Instead of 70 per cent, 85 per cent of the elected members of the province of Ontario were elected to support the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson. During his administration his policies had been altogether at variance with those of the party to which my hon. friend from Southeast Grey and her supporters belong. No members in or out of this house have a record such as his, and considering his record I think it is not very fitting that hon. members should speak of the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson as they have spoken of him in this house. I am one of his admirers and supporters and I feel that the affairs of the Dominion of Canada in Great Britain are safe in his hands. The Prime Minister of Canada is to be congratulated on making that selection and appointment.
Many times during this debate mention has been made of the present depression in our Dominion. It has been insinuated that the present government is responsible for that condition. The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) after telling the house that his was a rural riding, that the farmers in his constituency were noted for their thrift, and that the soil in South Perth was noted for its fertility, said that the farmers were very bitter towards the present administration because of the low prices they were receiving for their produce. He said that if there were an election at the present time the result would be different. I want to say to him that he and his colleagues should get down on their marrow bones and thank their Maker that the general election was held in the year 1930 	.
and not in 1931. If the election had been postponed until 1931 there would not have been enough Liberal members elected to form a corporal's guard. They would have been banished to the shades of opposition where they would have remained for a considerable time.
