speechtext: And will remain.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Southeast Grey made some comparison between the present depression and that existing between the years 1921 and 1924. In the comparison she stated that in the previous depression the high prices that the farmers received for their produce had provided them with a surplus with which they were able without serious effects to tide over the period of depression. She said that at the present time however they had no surplus and consequently they were in very bad straits indeed. On the other hand the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his address to this house dwelt at length on the prosperity of Canada during his administration, and quoted figures to support his contention. He gave figures concerning the amount of goods exported -from Canada in the year 1922, the first year of his administration. The right hon. gentleman told the house that in that year we exported $740,000,000 worth of goods. In 1923 the value of exports was $931,000,000; in 1924, $1,045,000,000; in 1925, $1,069,000,000; in 1926, $1,315,000,000; in 1927, $1,252,000,000; in 1928, $1,228,000,000; in 1929, $1,364,000,000, and in 1930, $1,120,000,000. In other words when the -present leader of the opposition came into power Canada's exports amounted to $2,000,000 daily, and during the last year he was in power they amounted to $3,000,000 daily. He stated further that when the policies of his government began to become effective there had been a surplus from year to year. His first surplus, -amounting to $36,000,000, occurred in the year 1924. From that he had a surplus every year until 1930 when the surplus was $47,740,000.
From this picture hon. members might think that Canada was in a very good condition financially, but the right hon. leader of the opposition did not give the house a full statement of the facts. He should have told the house the amount of goods imported into Canada during the same time. In the year 1922 the imports and exports were about the same in value. Exports were valued at $740,000,000 and imports at $748,000,000. The imports increased from year to year until the year 1930 when the goods imported into the Dominion of Canada amounting to $1,248,000,000. In other words when the present leader

The Address-Mr. Simpson (Simcoe)
of the opposition came into power the imports were about $2,000,000 daily and during the last year they were about three and one-half million dollars daily. To my mind that fact has had a very pronounced effect on the conditions in Canada at the present time. During the last year of the late administration we were selling goods valued at $3,000,000 daily and paying out three and one-half million dollars daily for imports. That is the results of the policy of the late administration. To that policy is to be attributed to a great extent the conditions existing in Canada to-day. We have been buying in other countries what we should have been producing and manufacturing at home.
The late administration claimed that they reduced taxes from year to year and still had a surplus. No government, institution or individual likes to end a year with a deficit. What advantage is it to the fruit growers in British Columbia, central Canada or the maritimes if by showing a surplus at the end of the year they are robbed of their market? When the product of the fruit growers is ready for the market he finds that his home market is flooded with fruit imported from other countries. Those countries on account of their fortunate geographical locations have climates in which fruit ripen earlier than it does in Canada, and those fruits are allowed to enter our country before our product is ready for the market. Under the late government they were allowed in under a small customs duty. The same statement may be made concerning manufacturers. What advantage is a surplus to the manufacturer if when his goods are ready for the market there is no home market for them? The same could be said concerning market gardeners and labourers. Goods may have been imported into Canada so as to create a surplus, but those imported goods may have caused the labourer to be out of a job in the factory where he had previously been employed. This is the effect:	If you buy an article
in a foreign country, you get the article and the foreign country gets your money. If you buy the same article at home you get the article and the money is kept in circulation in your own country. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) in his address the other day mentioned that the Dominion of Canada might be self-supporting and practically live within itself. I think we could do that to a very great extent, and that fact was very clearly illustrated by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis). He told the house that a large amount of barley was
for sale in western Canada, and he gave some comparisons which showed that tests made of Canadian barley and imported corn showed that barley was almost as good as the com for feeding purposes. I would commend that point very favourably to the feeders in Canada. Our own barley might be used in almost every case where corn is used at present, and by so doing we would keep circulating in our own country the money which we pay for feed. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) also mentioned the fact that more of our home grain might be used for feeding in our own country.
The fact that the increased tariff has been a benefit to Canada was very clearly illustrated by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson), the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Shaver) and by other members who have contributed to the debate. They cited concrete cases where factories had been opened and men were being employed at a good rate of wages because of the increases which were made in the tariff during the special session last September. I have here, sir, an article from one of our Ontario papers headed:
United States Newspaper Discusses Bennett Tariff
The article is as follows:
People in the United States are taking notice of what the Bennett tariff policy is doing for Canada. They realize that it has effectively safeguarded the Canadian market for Canadian workers without raising prices to consumers; they knowr that it is transferring a number of industries from their side of the international border to our side.
That is, from the United States to Canada. The article proceeds:
In neighbourly fashion the Times-Press says that it cannot regret Canada's good fortune and that it wishes the Dominion all progress and prosperity.
The article in the United States newspaper goes on to point out that every one of these new companies established in Canada is taking jobs from hard-pressed United States workmen in order to improve Canadian conditions. Then follows an appeal to the readers, many of whom are industrial workers, as follows:
Two American motor cars, formerly equipped with Akron-made tires, are to be made in Canada now. Their tires will be made in Canada and not by you. The men who earn wages by making those tires will be spending in Canadian stores and not in yours. They will be buying life insurance from Canadian agents and spending Canadian money to build and furnish homes, instead of patronizing v<w
662	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Simpson (Simcoe)
That is one of the results of the increased tariff. I would also like to read an editorial that was printed in one of our newspapers during the recent recess. It states:
The King government was turned out of office because it lacked constructive force, because it lacked vision and vigour. There were those who predicted that Mr. King would lead a much more useful opposition than he did a government. Even they must be disillusioned. His own marathon speech of twenty-seven thousand words offered not a single constructive thought to assist the Bennett administration to successfully meet present conditions. For nearly five hours Mr. King indulged in carping criticism, but not one concrete suggestion of helpful character did he venture.
It was evidently a Liberal "keynote" speech. For two weeks his supporters have entertained parliament and in all the records of Hansard their addresses show no more constructive nature than did that of their chief. They awakened to conditions in 1931 to which they had been blind for at least a year, but even with the awakening, they found no solution.
It begins to appear that in opposition, as in government. Mr. King has nothing to offer in the way of constructive statesmanship.
The hon. member for Macdonald, in his address this afternoon, mentioned the fact that in his riding there were quite a few hogs being fed on the cheap coarse grains of Manitoba, and he asked what would happen next autumn when those hogs were ready for market. I will answer him in this way: In Great Britain there is a market for all the bacon Canada can produce for some years to come. We will have to feed a great many more hogs than we are feeding at present if we are to over-stock that market. Great Britain imports over 900,000,000 pounds of bacon annually, and two-thirds of that amount is supplied by Denmark. When the late administration came into power Canada supplied over 200,000,000 pounds of bacon annually to the English market, but during last year that export almost ceased.
We in Canada should have a great advantage over the Danish farmer in the production of bacon, because at least eighty per cent of the grain fed to the hogs in Denmark is imported, and a great deal of that grain comes from North America, from the United States and Canada. When you consider the long freight haul of those grains it is plain that we should be able to produce bacon for very much less than it can be produced in Denmark, but to do so we will have to educate ourselves to the bacon requirements of the British market. Every hog between snout and tail will not produce Wiltshire sides, the kind of bacon required for the British market. A bacon hog requires a certain depth; it must have a certain length and depth of side; it must be not too thickly fleshed and not too 
lean. The people of Denmark, in order to produce that type of hog, went to a great deal of trouble to educate the farmers in the right type of hog to raise and also in the art of feeding, because breed in a bacon hog is not everything. The feeder has to have a certain knowledge of feeding before he can produce the required article.
There is in Great Britain a great future for the bacon industry of Canada; there is no reason why we should not supply at least half that 900,000,000 pounds of bacon imported annually by Great Britain. This is a matter which perhaps calls for assistance by the Department of Agriculture, but it cannot be done by that department alone. The hog producers of Canada must produce the article required by the British consumer. There is a great opportunity in this regard for cooperative pork packing establishments such as are operated in Denmark.
The hon. member for Macdonald said that in catering to the consumer it was necessary to supply quality products, and that statement applies very definitely to the production of bacon. You must supply an article of the right quality.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Myers), during his address the other evening, had something to say with reference to the production of potatoes in his province. What he said then applies also quite definitely to the potato growers in the province of Ontario. In my riding there is considerable land which is well suited to the production of potatoes. It is not every kind of land that will produce a good potato; the soil must possess certain qualities before it is possible to secure a good crop. When I was farming on my own account we did not pretend to grow potatoes in a commercial way; the soil was not suited to the purpose. But we grew enough for our own private use, and if possibly we produced them at a loss we were not, at any rate, driving on the roads consuming gas and wearing out the tires of cars. We stayed at home, and perhaps that was to our advantage.
I do not pretend to speak about the production of potatoes; I am concerned more with the market. I would ask the Department of Agriculture, in this connection, to insist upon the enforcement of the law regulating grading. I would make it an offence for anyone transporting potatoes on the highways by truck to any market if he failed, in the case of every sack of potatoes, to have a tag attached disclosing the grade of the potatoes and the name of the producer. One unscrupulous shipper from any district will do grave injury to the whole district, and there

2'he Address-Mr. Simpson (Simcoe)
are in my riding growers who are so particular in the shipment of their potatoes as always to have their produce a little over rather than under grade. When they offer potatoes for sale there is no difficulty about their securing a market; the wholesalers accept their potatoes without question, for they know that the producers can be depended upon, and they know that the purchasers will be satisfied. For this reason the market is continuous. I repeat, I would commend to the Department of Agriculture and the minister a rigid enforcement of the regulations in this respect.
A good deal has been said during this session about old age pensions; different hon. members have had something to say about the matter. We are not particularly concerned at this time with the question whether the old age pensions act was good legislation and ought to have been put on the statute books; the fact remains that it is there. AVe are not discussing to-night the reasons for its having been put there. Reading the reports of the proceedings of parliament in 1930, I read that the leader of the opposition made the statement that the system was a vicious one.
I could not make out precisely what he meant by its being a vicious system; I did not know whether he meant that it was a vicious principle to give pensions to old people, or that it was vicious for the Dominion of Canada to contribute a portion of the pension and allow the province to administer the act. At any rate, the act stands as we have it, and is in force in all the provinces except Quebec and the maritime provinces. Those provinces contribute to the amount paid by the Dominion government to Ontario and the western provinces, and in order to make the application of the principle general the Prime Minister in the campaign said that he would have the Dominion pay the full cost of pension. The leader of the opposition in his address stated that every old man and woman was promised full pension. The present act does not go that length, nor did I understand the Prime Minister to say that; the principle was only to be extended so as to cover the whole Dominion.
I have had something to do with the administration of the act in our county, and I think it leaves room for amendment in many respects. The old age pensions legislation is a good thing for many old people. Many of these old people were pioneers in this country; they hewed out homes for themselves, raised families, sometimes large families, and in some cases were unable to accumulate any property. The result is that now they have
grown old, and can no longer earn a livelihood as they formerly did, they are without means to support themselves. I know from experience in our own county that in many cases the provisions has been of great benefit to a good many of our old people, who have done more perhaps in building up the Dominion than many of those who at the present time are driving around in expensive cars. It is making their declining days a little easier for them, so that they need not worry about where their bread and butter will come from.
I might mention one case in the town of Barrie. One of the old pensioners was receiving $20 a month. He had no family; his wife was dead, and there was no one to look after him. He takes his pension, rents a room and provides his own food. He pays something like $10 a month for a heated room in winter and prepares and cooks his own meals, and he told me that in one month, doing this, he had saved $2 over and above providing for himself. He pays for his washing. He has a cleanly appearance and dresses comfortably, and he has been able to finance himself as I have stated. A man of that type should be made finance minister. But there are some things in the old age pensions act which to my mind could be amended, and when the legislation is brought down I shall have something to say with respect to certain of its provisions.
It is said that we are passing through a period of depression; and while the late government did not administer the affairs of the country in the best interests of the people, nevertheless we should not feel the pinch as we are feeling it now. There is something for the individual to do for himself: he should be given to understand that he must live within and not beyond his means. One thing which we as a people have not been doing is precisely this; we have not been living within our means. Consequently we are feeling the pinch particularly hard at the present time.
It has been said that the present government came into power at a very inopportune time. To my mind it came in at a very opportune time; for I believe that, with its policies, and taking hold of the problems of the Dominion as it is doing and managing them in a business way, we shall in due time have a prosperous, happy and contented people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As a new member addressing the house for the first time I respectfully ask the indulgence of this honourable assembly. I trust, Mr. Speaker, you will permit me to voice my appreciation of the dignity and fairness with
664	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Fraser (Northumberland) .
which you discharge the duties of your office, which sometimes must be a bit uncomfortable. Before proceeding, may I pause to express my deep regard for my French Canadian colleagues in this parliament. They lend much charm to the proceedings by the eloquence of their addresses.
I have the honour to represent, on this side of the house for the first time in over forty years, one of the most important agricultural, fruit-growing and industrial ridings in the province of Ontario-Northumberland county. Cobourg, the beautiful county town, is the most important deep water port between Kingston and Toronto, serving all central Ontario, and providing a year-round base for the twice-daily Canadian National car and passenger ferries between Canada and the United States. The people of Cobourg are vitally interested in the development of the St. Lawrence deep waterway and I am anxiously waiting any announcement by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) regarding this great and necessary undertaking.
I believe the people who elected me expected that I would make myself heard in this house both in the interest of my county and in the interest of this great Dominion, not as a narrow partisan but as a sincere Canadian citizen, endeavouring in his humble way to serve them and his country, to the best of his ability. This I intend to do according to my judgment.
I have followed with keen interest the proceedings of this house and the policies of this government, both here and in London. I have endeavoured at the same time to keep in touch with the people of my riding, and I can say most emphatically to this house that they are waiting for the Prime Minister to fulfil his many election promises. This, I believe he knows to his sorrow is beyond his capabilities to do. As a representative of the people, I believe it is my duty to assist if it is within my power to improve the conditions in Canada, and with this honest purpose in view, I submit for the consideration of this house my thoughts regarding our future. I believe we should have at this time definite suggestions to place before the administration for consideration and that wise counsels should prevail.
I disclaim any special knowledge of statesmanship, but with some knowledge of both business and public matters, I cannot see why the affairs of this country should not be conducted exactly as successful business is administered.
fW. A. Fraser.]
First, Mr. Speaker, I submit the greatest possibilities for trade expansion lie with Great Britain, and that the surest, safest and most logical place for us to concentrate our efforts, in peace as in war, is with the empire. Our policy should not be Canada alone, but Canada leading the way within the British commonwealth of nations for the advancement and security of all on which our welfare depends; in this way Canada can be first. A most illustrious citizen, speaking at a Canadian Club banquet in London, said that Canada was the cornerstone on which rests the great edifice of the empire. In this I fully agree. Let us live up to this position and make the edifice the greatest structure this world has ever known. In this way, and in this way alone, can we promote our Canadian interests in trade and commerce and make sure the safety of our future. In this way we develop markets with 460,000,000 people for our surplus agricultural and manufactured products; we will have our trade lanes protected by Great Britain, and we will be doing as much business as possible with the people on whom, in my opinion, will in the future depend the very existence of civilization as we know it. Canada, situated as it is, extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific, lying in the path of empire progress, with its great railway systems, vast natural resources, industrial centres, wonderful agricultural expansion and undaunted man power, must blaze the way.
Having had to make my living in business, I do not believe business can be done by blasting. I never blasted myself into a single order in twenty years, and never tried. Blasting only results in retaliation. I am a firm believer in the principle that business is done for mutual advantage. It is much easier to do business with friends than with strangers, and we generally do our utmost by friendly relations and the quality of our goods to increase our business with our best customers, especially when selling them twice as much as we buy from them. Business is a matter of give and take; nations are only collective individuals, and sometimes you have to give more for the present to get more in the future. It is poor business to antagonize your best -customers and seldom, if ever, .can you have all your own way. Alter all, the giving and taking must be pretty well 'balanced.
Never were trade relations between corporations and individuals maintained over a period of years except by -cordial understandings, plus mutual profit. I would like to quote, with commendation, the words of the Acting Prime

The Address-Mr. Fraser (Northumberland)
Minister of Japan, who, addressing the Canadian trade delegation at a farewell dinner in Tokyo a few months ago, said, in part:
Friendship is a greater thing than trade. Without it the springs of trade will be frozen. Trade can thrive only in a genial atmosphere of mutual good feeling, and friendship rests on knowledge.
The Prime Minister is a very able lawyer and has much to do with big business, but I doubt if he has had anything to do with actual salesmanship.
Let us take stock of Britain, the customer who bought $281,838,000 of products from us last year and sold us $189,180,000 worth. Britain, during the period of 1914 to 1919, stood the brunt of the world war, in which she suffered more than any other country. She sacrificed the flower of her manhood; she lost most of her foreign trade; she lost a large part of her shipping; she financed her allies and she is paying her war debts. Other countries, to supply the needs of their people previously supplied by Britain, built industries, many of them not adapted to the country in normal times, and they have since endeavoured to protect them with high tariff walls. The United States, with war profits and nearly forty per cent of the world's gold, a country over-industrialized, took advantage of Britain's position to make a drive to expand her foreign trade before the motherland could recover.
Where does Britain stand to-day? Last year Britain's overseas trade amounted to nine billion dollars-greater than any country except the United States, and greater than the United States in manufactured products. She built 35 per cent of the world's ships, and carried nearly 50 per cent of the world's shipping. She increased her foreign investments by over' a billion dollars and she developed at home the most efficient industrial system in the world. She has less unemployment pro -rata than that high protected country the United States, and had a favourable trade balance of $195,000,000. Far from being decadent, as the Hon. Howard Ferguson will learn, she is fast regaining her pre-war position.
When Britain succeeds, Canada succeeds. Britain is a trading nation, and while we need her as a consumer she is also necessary to us as a broker to resell our surplus, manufactured or otherwise. She is a clearing house for our products on the markets of the world, and more so now than in the past.
World conditions are changing. The importance of Russia as a competitor is becoming more serious. As so well stated by His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales when opening the British industrial exhibition at Buenos Aires, artificial trade barriers which are
a menace to commerce to-day must be modified and the world economic system must be readjusted. Let us get together with Britain, before she is forced into further trade treaties with European and other foreign countries by our foolish Canada-alone policy, with its blasting methods which have made it more impossible for her to do business with us, and join the other dominions in working out the possibilities of increasing our trade within the empire, so there can be control for the benefit of the whole, even if it hurts in spots.
I submit for the consideration of this government for the adjourned Imperial economic conference the following proposal:	that a
non-political empire trade council be formed, comprising the following members from Britain and each dominion: one government representative, one outstanding industrialist, one outstanding financier, one prominent agriculturist, one outstanding economist, one outstanding transport man, and one outstanding labour representative, to study the foreign trade of their respective countries and the possibilities of encouraging the exchange of commodities with other parts of the empire; the council to meet in London within twelve months, to draft recommendations to be considered and acted upon by their different governments, these recommendations to include tariff readjustments, trade treaties, and other arrangements that they consider will further develop empire trade.
There is something like $14,000,000,000 of trade annually within the British Empire. Britain has the same right to determine her policy as Canada has. The Prime Minister knows we cannot dictate the course she is to follow; she knows her business better than we do, but she will welcome sane, reciprocal trade considerations as will our sister dominions. Britain protects our ocean trade lanes and the empire has a great world responsibility at this time.
I submit for the consideration of the government that a thorough investigation be made to devise ways and means of diverting a greater percentage of our overseas trade through Canadian ports. Last year $205,163,170, or 34 per cent of our overseas exports, and $9,849,889 of our imports, were handled by United States ports. Canada has excellent port facilities on bath the Atlantic and the Pacific where millions of dollars have been invested. Railway rates should be so adjusted as to divert the traffic through these gateways instead of through United States ports. If this is done, it will certainly help to solve the problem of unemployment. Our railways are laying off men. They need the
656	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Fraser (Northumberland)
traffic, ouv terminal men require this work, and the sooner Canadian freight is handled by Canadians in Canada, the sooner will more of our people find employment. The Canadian railways should increase their proportion of through freight rates with United States railways. I submit to the Minister of Railways and Canals that is one of the most important policies in connection with the transportation problem in the Dominion of Canada. It is absolutely necessary for Canada to find markets for her products and to increase her foreign trade in order to cure unemployment. This can best be accomplished within the empire, with the assistance and cooperation of Britain. The influence and benefit of trade must be considered fairly in all its ramifications, and not only from a manufacturing viewpoint. The handling of imports as well as exports provides work and increases business, and in some oases much more labour is employed in handling imported commodities from the seaboard to the consumer than would be used to manufacture the same commodities in Canada. The use of Canadian raw materials and the amount of labour employed should be the yardstick of tariff protection.
I am going to issue on the floor of the house a warning in connection with protection. If the manufacturers of Canada seek and procure increased protection from the government, then the government-and this thought applies to every administration-should procure from the protected Canadian manufacturers the assurance that they will consider and put into practice the purchase of Canadian materials for every branch of their operation. Protected Canadian manufacturers should realize that the responsibility lies with them to protect and to give to Canadian labour every advantage of their protection. In this I mean not only the labour that is employed in turning out their own product, but the Canadian labour that is employed or that it is possible to employ in the production of every article that is used in their industry. My contention is that many Canadian manufacturers are free traders when they are purchasing the materials that enter into the products of their factories and protectionists when they are selling the products of those factories to the Canadian public. I am not making in this house statements that I am not in a position to verify and I state emphatically that the perspective of many Canadian manufacturers is narrow and selfish; it is antiCanadian and diametrically opposed to the policy they themselves advocate. They wish to help with employment, if they can use [Mr. W. A. Fraser.}
men profitably in their own industry, but they do not give a thought to the number of Canadians who could obtain work if they purchased as much Canadian material as possible on equal terms from other Canadian manufacturers and producers.
I agree with the Prime Minister that this is a time for action; it is a time for sane, logical and consistent action. The republic to the south of us has made it harder and harder for us to get the products of our farms and factories into their country, yet the Canadian manufacturers continue to play into the hands of United States industry. Like the Prime Minister I feel that it is a time for plain speaking and clear thinking as to the economic policy of this country and its political effect, particularly as regards Great Britain and the empire of which we are proud to form a part. First let us put our own house in order, then let us strengthen the empire so that we can in part, and as a whole, formulate a policy that will promote the interests of the British commonwealth of nations, if necessary against the rest of the world.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, unemployment will cease only when our trade increases. I have endeavoured to place before this house three definite ways in which employment of labour in Canada can be increased. Within the empire we have every product and commodity that is required by the people of the empire to trade. Britain is a naturally industrial and trading country; Canada has vast resources but is immature, and will naturally be so for many years to come until our population is capable of consuming a greater proportion of the product of our industries and until our population is so distributed as to lessen the distances that exist between populated centres. Our policies will have to be worked out slowly. No one has more confidence in the future of Canada than I, but we are not quite in a position to dictate to Great Britain what she shall do, and certainly we should not attempt it as long as we rely on the British navy to protect our overseas commerce. I believe in Canada as being allimportant in service and strength to the empire. Our population is made up of descendants of the two great peoples of the world, the British and the French, and we are capable of leading the way within the empire. The union of the United States on one side and the progress of soviet Russia on the other is forcing an economic alliance of the countries of Europe. A lowering of trade restrictions between the countries of Europe will mean a further decrease of Canadian trade with these countries. As a Canadian citizen and a mem-

The Address-Mr. Both well
ber of this house I state emphatically that it is the essential duty of this government to have ready to submit at the economic conference to be held in Ottawa this coming summer, definite proposals that will be acceptable to Great Britain and the other parts of the empire, for the increase of trade within ourselves.
I submit that the Prime Minister will have to change the attitude he adopted at the London conference, and I suggest that he adopt the attitude of the Hon. Charles Dunning when he said, in part:
We do not intend to meet the other countries of the British commonwealth of nations in a spirit of petty bargaining, but rather in a broad spirit of willingness to become in ever increasing measure good customers to those who treat us in like manner. This is the spirit in which we desire to meet all nations, but we believe that within the British commonwealth of nations lies the greatest measure of opportunity for development of trade, because of our common heritage, kindred institutions and a common patriotism.
A man who considers his own interest and his own interest alone, seldom succeeds; never over the long run, and it is not otherwise with nations.
With all the emphasis that I can express I desire to say that it is the bounden obligation of the present government to make sure that the economic conference to be held in Ottawa during the coming summer will be productive of ways and means whereby we can solidify the British Empire in trade as well as in sentiment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in this debate in the belief that it is necessary for each member of the house to bring to the attention of the government the situation as he sees it in his own constituency so that conditions in all parts of the country may be placed before the government. Everybody realizes that we are going through difficult times. No one I think blames any particular party in Canada for that. Parties may be to some extent responsible but we have a world-wide condition that must also be considered, and we must realize that no party can solve in a few days the difficulties which confront us. During the election campaign last July many of the electors in Canada I believe supported Conservative candidates in the various provinces on account of the pledges that were given at that time by leaders of the Conservative party. The people realized that Canada was in much the same position as some of the other countries in the world, and they believed that the promises that were made by the leaders of the Conservative party
throughout Canada would be carried out. Instead of going over many of the promises that were made to the electors in my constituency,
I should like to give in a sentence or two some of the representations that were made by the Conservative party's candidates in appealing to the voters of that constituency.
This is an advertisement that appeared in the press: "Bennett will win on July 28. Why? He will sell Canada's wheat crop. He will solve the unemployment situation. He will build a highway across Canada. He will keep Canadian trade for Canada and make employment for your sons and daughters." Just what influence that advertisement may have had on the electors of the constituency I do not know, but I believe that it had considerable. In any event the electors there were entitled to take at their word those who were responsible for that advertisement and expect that those pledges would be carried out. I want to deal for a moment with some of those pledges and see what has been done by the government of the day to carry them out.
We have looked in vain for any move on the part of the government that will sell Canada's wheat crop. We in the west who are dependent upon wheat have not been able to see that the government of the day has done anything to assist in disposing of our wheat crop. We still have our wheat, and we have not found a market for it. There is possibly an intimation in the speech from the throne that something along that line is going to be done. The speech in one paragraph says:
My government has explored the origins of our difficulties and is firmly of the belief that many of our problems do not arise out of world-wide depression, but are antecedent to it; and that domestic factors have also largely determined the degree of economic distress from which this country is suffering.
That may mean that the government believe that they have found a solution for some of those difficulties. The speech from the throne also says:
My ministers have had under anxious consideration the means by which an orderly marketing of the wheat crop of western Canada may be assured, and have already taken such effective action towards that end as the circumstances appear to justify. My ministers are aware that changing conditions in the world's markets may necessitate further intervention by my government, which is prepared to render whatever additional assistance may be deemed advisable in the national interest.
That, I say, contains an intimation that something will be done to enable Canada to dispose of her wheat, but up to the present time we fail to see that anything has actually been done. W'heat is to-day at almost its

Mr. Bennett, departing for Britain, expressed confidence in his mission, and up to the very end, when the failure of the conference became clear to all, faith existed that somehow he would induce the British government to purchase the bulk of the dominion's wheat surplus.
Mr. Bennett within the restricted ground of his "Canada first" policy, undoubtedly did his best. His offer to the British people of a preference in Canadian markets, based upon a 10 per cent increase in the duties upon all foreign products, was sincere. The weakness of the plan, so far as the British people were concerned, was that while it involved a guarantee that the British would buy Canada's wheat, there was no corresponding guarantee that the Canadian people would buy British goods. Everybody looked forward with hopefulness to that meeting on December 30 in the city of Regina. Swift Current, Sask.,
January 2nd, 1931.
The Hon. Robert Weir,
Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir:
_ The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, in bis address in Regina on the 30th ultimo intimated that a scheme had been worked out for enabling farmers of the west to get into diversified farming through governmental assistance.
That was the way I understood the Prime Minister's address.
I have a letter from one of my constituents to-day, Walter Smith of Beaver Flats, Saskatchewan, stating that he listened to Mr. Bennetf's address over the radio and he wants to be among the first to take advantage of the scheme. In his letter he mentions that I will, no doubt, have the particulars and he wished me to advise him just what the scheme is, and forward to him the necessary application forms.
I would be glad to have any information you can give me in this connection so that I can advise Mr. Smith.
That letter was written on January 2. On January 14, a letter was written to me by the Minister of Agriculture as follows:
[Mr Bothwell.]
Assistance to farmers in the nature of seed grain, etc.. I understand, will be made through the machinery of the provincial government as they are closer to the problem and will save the Dominion government a good deal of expense in duplicating machinery.
I hope hon. members listened to the reading of my letter and the reading of the letter in reply from the Minister of Agriculture. There is not a single word in that reply with reference to the questions which I asked. However, the minister stated that he understood that assistance in the nature of seed grain would be made through the machinery of the provincial governments. I wanted to know then what the provincial government knew about this plan which had been announced by the Prime Minister, so I wrote to Regina. The provincial legislature was then in session and a question was put on the orders of the day in order to find out what they knew about the situation. This was the question:
Have arrangements been made by the federal government with the provincial government in connection with implementing the promise made by the Hon. R. B. Bennett, in bis address at Regina on December 30, 1930, of assistance to farmer's in securing seed grain, etc.?
The answer was:
Discussions have taken place between members of the Dominion government and the provincial government regarding seed grain, and information is being asked for rural municipalities in order that appropriate action may be taken.
So still I had no information. To-day, Mr. Speaker, a question was asked of the Prime Minister as to how this finance company, or whatever it is to be called, was getting along, but apparently as yet it is not functioning, and we do not know whether or not it ever will function. In any event, if I understood correctly the answer given on the floor of the house to-day, there has been no relief of any kind given to any farmer at any place in Canada under the scheme announced by the Prime Minister last December. As a matter of fact, I believe that speech was made by the right hon. gentleman following a speech made by Mr. Beatty in London, Ontario, on December 5, when Mr. Beatty said:
To me, an unprejudiced and unofficial but not disinterested observer, it seems indisputable the Dominion government should not hesitate to intervene with an offer of assistance as a national public duty. In recent years assistance, as I have indicated, lias been given in one way or another for the removal of disabilities of manufacturing interests, of the dairy and fruit farmers of the east and British Columbia, and of the maritime provinces. More recently direct financial aid has been provided for unemployed workers. Special pro-

The Address-Mr. Bothwell
vision for the farmers of the west, suffering from difficulties which they could not foresee nor avoid, should be regarded by other groups in the country as a simple act of justice.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, although we had the definite promise that the Conservatives would sell our Canadian wheat, they went to the conference and fell down. We had the announcement in Regina on December 30 of last year that some assistance would be given to the west right away, but outside of some seed grain and possibly some gasoline provided through the municipalities there has been no relief of any kind, so far as I know, given to the west other than what assistance they received under that $20,000,000 unemployment relief bill. In that connection, I do not know but what the position to-day is worse than it was before the 820,000,000 was voted. It seems to me it is going to be impossible for the municipalities of the west to carry through such unemployment schemes again. Any person who observed the public works that were being carried on last winter under the scheme must have come to the conclusion that the municipalities could have done the work just as efficiently and as well for the amount of money they themselves were spending, without the assistance which was granted by the provincial or federal governments. That added assistance was simply being used by the workmen in order, shall I say, to lie down on the job. The work did not progress as it should. I believe it would have been cheaper for Canada if the unemployed had been put on direct relief instead of working under that Unemployment Relief Act.
I did not and do not now object to the appropriation of $20,000,000; I believe it to be the duty of this government to take steps to remedy the unemployment situation in Canada. If this cannot be done by governmental policies, then it will be necessary to do it by appropriations, because we cannot allow people in Canada to starve when we have all kinds of food in the country. However, realizing the difficulty with which the west is faced; with the western premiers coming down to Ottawa; with farmer organizations from one end of the country to the. other sending in resolutions and with deputations of farmers coming to Ottawa pleading with the government to fix the price of wheat, why was not something done? They did not hesitate in 1.917 and 1918 to peg wheat prices. They did not hesitate then when it was in the interests possibly of other people to handle our wheat. We do not know yet whether the allies got the benefit of the reduced price or whether the government got it. None of the questions asked on
the orders of the day have been answered. Ever since I have been in the house my experience has been that most of the questions asked on the orders of the day, in the course of routine proceedings, would have been answered. To-day, if you ask a minister the amplest kind of question he says, "Put it on the order paper"; and we'have not been able to receive answers to important questions asked in this house, any more than I was able to get answer to the questions which I submitted on January 2. It is time that hon. members in this house brought forcibly to the attention of the government the situation which Canada is in at the present time, and demanded some action. We believe it is the duty of this government to fix the price of wheat if they cannot do anything else. Are they not in a position to enable us to sell our wheat at fair prices after we have contributed to the manufacturers from one end of the country to the other since the inception of these tariff regulations? Surely they cannot expect us after that to go down tc defeat in the west and abandon that country just because, in a year or two of stress, the government will not come to our assistance and fix a price.
Last winter, organizations of various kinds throughout western Canada held meetings at different points, and I myself have a record of forty-three different meetings held in the constituency of Swift Current. Resolutions were passed at these meetings. I did not attend any of them with the exception of a board of trade meeting at Swift Current; but as I say, at all these meetings resolutions were adopted and forwarded to the government. I received copies of them-resolutions from boards of trade, village and rural councils, farmers' organizations and so on. Let me quote one resolution which was adopted at Pennant, Saskatchewan, on December 17, 1930, requesting that certain things be done:
1.	That the federal government guarantee a minimum fixed price of wheat for this year's crop at one dollar ($1) per bushel f.o.b. Fort William.
2.	That a board of standards be set up whose duty it will be to arrive at a proper relationship between the price which the farmer has to pay for the commodities which he purchases and the price which he receives for the commodities which he has to sell.
3.	That we urge the nationalization of currency and credit.
4.	That we demand a moratorium until such time as proper adjustments have been made.
5.	That the legal rate of interest at 7 per cent as set out in the Bank Act be enforced, and that no one shall be allowed to charge higher than the legal rate of interest.
The Address-Mr. Bothwell

6.	That the federal government, in conjunction with the provincial governments, institute a form of crop insurance.
7.	That we ask for the nationalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the re-valuation of the Canadian National.
8.	That we continue our efforts to secure for the growers 100 per cent control of the marketing of their products; first, by demanding that a grain marketing act, as suggested by the wheat pool, be placed on the statutes; secondly, that a primary products act be placed on the
. statutes.
This is the type of resolution which was passed at each of these forty-three meetings. The resolutions vary in some respects, but so far as I know there has never been received, from any member of the government, an answer to a single one of these resolutions forwarded here since December last. I cannot tell to whom the various resolutions were sent, but I have copies of them. They were directed to the attention of the government but there have been no replies.
Now, we are immersed in spring work at this season of the year and the farmers have been looking for some information from the government. They wish to know what they are to do. They do not know whether or not to seed a crop. The weather conditions are not propitious, and in any event they are taking a chance in sowing a crop. Surely, then, they are entitled to some encouragement from the government of the day in order that they may react favourably, so to speak, to the weather conditions as they are. But they can gelt no information. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that a number of these questions that are asked on the orders of the day should be answered without our having to wait for replies through the ordinary publications of the house. These questions should be answered on the floor of the house; they are questions that concern the farmers throughout the west. Hon. members desire to send information to their constituents but they cannot do so, and it matters not whether you go to the department or ask questions on the floor of the house, you do not seem to be able to obtain any information.
I have here a letter written on April 2, and in this connection I wish the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) were in his place to hear it. I should not like hon. members of this house to believe that the conditions throughout the west are as the hon. member for Marquette would have us understand. The letter in question is dated, at Swift Current, Saskatchewan, April 2, 1931, and is addressed thus:

Hon. R. J. Manion,
Minister of Railways, Ottawa.
Hon. J. A. Merkley,
Minister of Railways, Regina.
C. E. Bothwell, K.C.. M.P., Ottawa.
Hon. W. W. Smith, M.L.A., City.
Re-South Saskatchewan Railway and Traffic
Bridge and Southwestern Saskatchewan Development
Honourable Gentlemen:
Adverting to our previous resolutions a memorandum of which is enclosed; and as the estimates will soon be up for consideration at Ottawa and in view of the continuation of present depressed condition of agriculture, labour and business, it is imperative that some projects be undertaken in this city and district to relieve the unemployment situation, augment the circulation of money, bring about needed facilities and maintain a spirit of confidence and encouragement of our people to say nothing of absolute want and poverty of a very great section of our people. Our board most urgently request that further relief of some kind be found as other relief measures are now exhausted being only temporary relief and that now larger projects must be undertaken to enable people to earn a livelihood and at the same time afford the district and city service facilities that will be of use for all time.
The letter goes on to refer to railway construction works that should be proceeded with, such as are indicated in the resolutions that were sent down and in the corresipondence alluded to in the letter. I wish to bring this matter to the attention of the government in order that they may realize, if they have not already done so, that the situation in the west is indeed serious and that it is time something was done to encourage the people in that part of the country, especially at this time of the year when they feel that, if they are to have anything to live on this winter, they must put in a crop. They are entitled to the information they require if they are to realize out of their crop enough to pay expenses.

In discussing the speech from the throne and the amendment thereto proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) I am not unmindful that Canada is going through one of the severest world-wide economic depressions she has ever known- this in spite of the fact that during the last election campaign Conservative candidates in the eastern townships of Quebec claimed that this depression was due entirely to the administration of the late government. I do not wish for one moment, Mr. Speaker, that you should consider me a pessimist. I am not in the least a pessimist. I know that of all countries in the world Canada, with all its troubles, is possibly best off at the present

The Address-Mr. Howard
time. With our undeveloped natural resources; with our hard-working, thrifty, kind-hearted population; with our increasing gold production and our enormous mining possibilities, to say nothing of our agricultural areas, which are second to none, we shall emerge from this crisis as we have emerged from similar situations in the past; and I am perfectly satisfied that when we get out of this depression conditions in Canada will be better than they have ever been before.
As to my own section of the country, I believe, notwithstanding the general depression that exists there also, and especially in Sherbrooke, that we are possibly better off than any place else in Canada. In my remarks, therefore, what I wish to prove is that the promises made during the last election campaign by the Conservative party have not been kept, and that the way in which the present government is handling the affairs of the country is retarding the comeback into our regular stride. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and other hon. members of this house have shown where these policies might carry us in our empire relations, but I want to show this house how the policies of the present government have affected my own constituency in southern Quebec.
I am not a protectionist Liberal, as most people say I am, nor am I a free trade Liberal, as others think I am, but I believe that free trade is just as bad for Canada as is the present high protection. The only policy which will benefit this country in the long run, or even at the present time, is one which is between the two extremes, one on a par with the old Liberal policy.

I think credit is due to
the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) for his sincerity, because I believe he is sincere in his ideas of what is best for Canada. But I do think, and I shall attempt to prove my argument in the short time at my disposal, that his policies are detrimental both to my own section and to Canada as a whole. The present government is in power for two reasons: First, because of the extraordinary unemployment situation which existed, and second, the falling prices of farm products, which prevailed at the time of the elections. I will not quote the many promises made by the Prime Minister, but I do want to refer to some remarks he made at a meeting held in my home town. The following is a quotation
from the paper which supported the present government during the last elections^ the Sherbrooke Daily Record, and I would particularly call the attention of the house to it:
What is the use of advertising in the town paper that John Smith is sick, without sending ior the doctor? Send for the doctor. He is the Conservative party.
The following is a remark made by the Prime Minister at that same meeting:
Canadians want the right to work and when a government fails to correct the causes of unemployment over which it has control that government can justly be charged with negligence.
The other Sherbrooke paper, La Tribune, which supported the Liberal party, in reporting that same meeting said:
Vte wish to call a special session to put an end to these conditions, because the people want work and not doles.
Bennett:	Exactly. What you want is
work and not a conference. I am not making you pledges, lightly. Should I not keep them, J ask the members who you elect to withdraw irom me their support.
This meeting was reported- to have been attended by about 12,000 people. It was held in the 54th armouries, which is situated in the centre of the industrial section of Sherbrooke. The Prime Minister then became more brave, walked to the front of the platform, pointed in the direction of one of the industries, and said: "I know I am speaking within a stone's throw of some of the finest industries in Canada; I know that those industries are on short time, and if I am elected on July 28, within thirty days the men, women and children will be going back to those industries and getting the work they should get." Mr. Speaker, two hundred and sixty-two days have expired instead of thirty and the situation is worse than it has ever been.
In the city of Sherbrooke there are 42 industries. Without taking particular examples, I desire to give the house certain information in connection with twelve of the main industries in the city of Sherbrooke.
In 1930, one of our specialty steel companies employed 125 hands, and on February 15, 1931, their employment had dropped to 100 hands.
Our largest steel manufacturing industry employed 488 hands in July of 1930; in February of this year, their payroll had dropped to 400.
One of our cotton industries employed 363 hands in July, 1930, while to-day they are employing only 323.
Another specialty steel industry employed 150 as against 125 to-day.

The Address-Mr. Howard

Another company's payroll dropped from 70 to 58.
Another large steel company was employing 119 hands only fifteen days before the last election, and on February 15 last, they were employing only 27; from 119 to 27.
A rubber company dropped from 80 to 65 and another machinery company from 30 to 10.
A silk company employing 490 in July of last year was employing that number in February of this year but it was working on shorter hours. The same would apply to other companies.
From the date of the elections to the present day there has been a decrease in employment affecting 321 hands. Most important of all, these same industries have dropped from 149,174 weekly hours to 106,904, or a slackening off of 42,270 hours per week. Figured at the ordinary price paid for labour, that represents a shrinkage in the payroll of 12 out of a total of 42 industries, amounting to over $12,000 per week. In other words, over $12,000 per week less money is being paid out to-day in the city of Sherbrooke than was being paid when the promises were made by the present Prime Minister that the unemployment situation would be cured.
In another section, close to Sherbrooke, where is produced one of the articles of which Canada boasts of controlling a large percentage of the world's supply, the candidates stated on all the hustings that because Mr. R. B. Bennett was connected with the big business men of Canada he would supply with his friends the necessary capital to put these mines on their feet as they had never been before. I do not intend to discuss this situation because the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) will probably do so, but in Thetford Mines to-day they are producing asbestos at the lowest rate ever prevailing since the Conservatives were last in power. More than that, in the town of Black Lake, not one single mine is operating and the asbestos industry is practically ruined in that section.
If the Prime Minister were in his seat I would direct his attention to the statement he made yesterday on the floor of this house. He said that he would never consent to unemployment insurance, but I say to-night that if the manufacturers of Canada have to take on unemployment insurance in the near future they can date the cause back to the present government's attitude towards the needs of this country.
I have every respect for the hon. Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson); he is a personal friend of mine, but I say that the Minister of Labour of the government of

I have covered my last point and that is the reduced purchasing power. The other day I was riding on the train and went into the smoking car where there were six other men discussing that most popular question, the existing situation. They were discussing what this government was doing, what the other government had not done, and so forth, and one of them said, "Can you tell me why, with eggs at 15 cents a dozen and all other farm products at the lowest prices they have been for years, the people do not start to buy and live on these products?" I leave it to any man in this house to say how many eggs or how much lamb or pork or any other food a man with five children and a wife to support could buy with $8.88 for a week's work. Do you know what they have to do, Mr. Speaker?-and I am proud to say that they can do it. They buy a big piece of heavy meat, with the bone in the centre, a piece of extra good quality at the lowest price, and of that they make the most nourishing food, which is soup, and they buy bread and use it without butter, hoping for the time when the Liberal government will be back in power again and men will get at least a living wage.
In case some hon. gentlemen may think that these cases are overdrawn, let me say that I am not speaking of men who started to work only a few weeks ago. A man recently came to my office who had been in the service of a certain company for sixteen years. He was a sober, hard-working, industrious man, and for sixteen years, almost the best part of his life, he had been working for that same concern. He worked fifty-five hours and he drew $15 for a whole week's pay, after sixteen years of faithful service. Before the last election that same man, doing the very same job for the very same company, drew a minimum of from $23 to $25 a week, so there was a shrinkage of $10 a week in his pay since this government came into office. When the previous government was in power he was running two slubbers in a cotton mill; to-day he is running four slubbers at a reduced wage of $10 per week. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that these are things that make one wonder where we are going to get off at.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, speaking in this house the other evening, took a great deal of credit for industries which he said had recently been established in the town of Farnham. Everybody rejoices when new industries come into our towns, especially in the eastern townships; but let us have the facts as they are. One of those industries, is a plush
[Mr. Howard.1
factory. It was established in the town of Farnham in 1929, under the administration of my right hon. leader who now sits on this side of the house. Another industry is the big linoleum concern. That was astablished in 1930, before the present government came into power, before it was ever dreamed that it would come into power. The other industry is the silk factory. It is true that that factory in the hon. gentleman's riding is fairly prosperous, but he did not tell this house that this silk company got an increased protection, and reduced the wages of every man 25 per cent. The men went on strike, and they only came back to work two weeks ago Monday at the reduced rate. The enamel industry, the only other industry in that part of the country, was started back in 1922, under the administration of my right hon. leader. My hon. friend had a special way of conducting his campaign. I suppose anybody can conduct his campaign as he sees fit, but speaking at Knowlton he said, "To hell with the national debt, but let us do something for the farmers." I ask him now what has this government done for the farmers of his constituency. Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, since the twelfth day of last month I have listened to about ninety speeches. I am somewhat loath to address the house. My reluctance is not entirely due to diffidence, nor is it attributable to a belief that all has been said which can be usefully said. I find it more interesting to listen. It was not my intention to speak during this debate but my good intentions have yielded to the provocation-or inspiration-of the words which have fallen from the lips of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard). He and I have the advantage of coming from a part of the country which, in common with all who have visited it, we believe to be the most beautiful part of the whole Dominion. It is interesting for reasons other than its topography. It is a thumb nail of Canada; .vith the possible exception of deep sea fishing there is to be found within those half dozen counties the entire range of activity of the whole Canadian people. There lumbering, farming, mining, milling, industry in factories, trade in the shops, finance, and transportation engage the attention of an active and energetic people. Moreover there is in the population a diversity of origin and outlook which makes for nicety and consideration in the relationships between man and man.
My hon. friend from Sherbrooke has spoken of this miniature Canada; he has told us his version of conditions prevailing there. My friendship for the hon. gentleman is not of yesterday, he knows that my feelings for him are both deep and sincere, but I now have for him a feeling of profound commiseration if lie believes all he has said to-night, and if he believes that all he has said is all that may be said with regard to conditions in the eastern townships. Mr. Speaker, why does my hon. friend draw a veil over his remarks? Why does he refer to industries and individuals in hazy and indefinite language? For the benefit of the house, and to establish accuracy and truth, I shall endeavour to place upon the record the names of corporations and individuals who to-day are infinitely better off and whose hundreds of employees are better off as a result of the policies of the present government.

My hon. friend has told us there is a tool company in Sherbrooke which is not doing much work. That is true. The Rand Drill Company specializes in mining equipment, and unfortunately, due to over-production, the mining industry is not being carried on as actively as it has been in years past. Because there is no demand for mining equipment there is no work for the Rand Drill Company. Is the government to blame for that? My hon. friend has told us there is a cotton mill in Sherbrooke not doing much work. Without doubt he refers to the Sherbrooke Cotton Mills-a large part of whose output is fabric used in the manufacture of automobile tires. Because there is slight activity in the automobile manufacturing industry.
